I’m sure he will just help us out of the kindness of his twisted little heart and not, you know, put the rest of us through the wringer too .” Jake flinched slightly at her anger. She wasn’t totally off, though. He’d already gone through all of that in his head—and worse. And the solution still sat there like a lead weight on his chest. This was going to be a risk. He inhaled, slow and steady, trying to quiet the hammering in his blood. His voice, when it came, was flat and final. “One of you finish the half-done gen by the central room. The other goes to the exit gate. As soon as it's powered, you leave. Don’t wait for me.” Claudette’s eyes widened. “Jake. No. You saw what he did to Leon. He’s angry . You’ve been his primary target all match. If you go near him—” “That’s exactly why I have to,” his voice was sharper than intended, trying to sound more confident than he felt. “He’s not gonna listen to you. Or Meg. But me? He’s been hunting me since I interrupted his game. That’s leverage.” Meg looked like she was biting her own tongue, trying to resist the urge to explode again. “You think you can get him to agree to help? To just... grow a conscience all of a sudden?” "He doesn’t need a conscience. He just needs a reason." She stared at him, open-mouthed for a second, then threw her hands in the air. “Jake, and I say this with all the love in the world, but that is the stupidest thing you’ve ever said.” “What other option do we have?” he snapped back. “Do you want to drag Leon to the gate and hope the Fog decides he’s worth saving? Do you want to guess what happens to someone who dies outside the trials? You think the campfire’s gonna magically fix this? ” He was breathing hard now. The adrenaline was coming back, his tone rising sharp with the pressure behind his ribs He looked down at his hand — still stained with flecks of key rust, cold against his skin. “He’s been on me all match. Ignoring you two. Testing me. Luring me out. That’s something I can use .” Claudette stepped in again, trying to keep him grounded. “You don’t even know if Herman will agree to anything. He could just kill you. Or both of you.” “I know.” “Jake—” He held up a hand, voice cracking slightly from the strain. “I know. Okay? I know. But we don’t have another play. And you know it.” Before they could argue, before Meg could slap some guilt into him or Claudette could plead for a better answer, Jake turned and started walking. Everything in him wanted to run the other way. But someone had to fix this. And it had to be him. Chapter 7: Terms and Conditions Jake crept from room to room, listening for any sign of Herman’s presence. He didn’t need to be stealthy — not for what he had planned—but he wasn’t in a rush to blow the others’ cover before he even knew if this would work. Deep down, though, he knew that wasn’t the real reason. He was stalling. Dragging his feet, hiding in corners, circling the drain. This was insane , no matter how he looked at it. He had caught the faint edges of the Doctor’s terror radius a few rooms back, hovering just at the perimeter like a rabbit watching the edge of a snare. Close enough to start acclimating. Far enough to pretend he could still back out. Jake ran the options again — third time? fourth? — desperately hoping to find a loophole he’d somehow missed. Some clever workaround. Anything other than this. Because yeah, sure, technically he’d be fine in the end. Just another pop back to the campfire, same as always. But the Doctor was a sadist. And this time , Jake was handing himself over willingly. He wasn’t stupid. He knew exactly what that meant. Somewhere behind him, there was the faintest creak of movement — quiet footsteps echoing his own, far enough back to stay out of sight. One of the girls was trailing him, ready to slip in to help if the deal was accepted. They’d figured out who was running the gate and who was staying, then. Good. Smart of them to keep out of view until the last possible second. If this went sideways, no reason for all three of them to go down together. Jake slowed. Listened. He could still hear Herman pacing in a loose arc — stalking nearby, probably trying to flush them toward the generator hallway. The last three were clustered together, too tempting a target for a killer to ignore. He could keep circling. Keep dancing just out of reach. Or he could suck it up and go. He took one steadying breath, set his jaw, and stepped around the corner — out into the open. Herman was done with this trial. The only thing keeping him from quitting the whole charade outright was the gnawing pressure of the Entity’s eyes still fixed squarely on his spine. He’d had one of the pests locked down — neutralized far more efficiently than just bleeding out in the hallway — but the girls had vanished like smoke, and the one survivor he would have liked to disembowel personally was proving to be the single most aggravating little shit he’d dealt with in weeks. Sabotage at every turn. Flitting through his territory like a cockroach with ADHD. Breaking equipment, baiting chases, mocking him. It was enough to make his static flare just thinking about it.
